questions.stem: In hydrogen spectrum, the ratio of wavelengths of the last line of Lyman series and that of the last line of Balmer series is
questions.solution:
Step 1: The last (series-limit) line has $n_2 \to \infty$, so $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\frac{1}{n_1^{2}}\right)$.
Step 2: Lyman ($n_1 = 1$): $\frac{1}{\lambda_L} = R$. Balmer ($n_1 = 2$): $\frac{1}{\lambda_B} = \frac{R}{4}$.
Step 3: $\frac{\lambda_L}{\lambda_B} = \frac{1/R}{4/R} = \frac{1}{4} = 0.25$.
Final Answer: (C) 0.25
Quick Tip: Series-limit wavelengths scale as $n_1^{2}$: Lyman : Balmer : Paschen $= 1 : 4 : 9$.

questions.stem: For a perfectly black body, coefficient of emission is
questions.solution:
Step 1: Coefficient of emission (emissivity) $e$ is the ratio of the energy radiated by a body to that radiated by a perfectly black body at the same temperature.
Step 2: For the perfectly black body itself this ratio is $1$; it is the best possible emitter (and absorber).
Final Answer: (B) unity.
Quick Tip: $0 \le e \le 1$; $e = 1$ only for a perfect black body (good absorbers are good emitters).

questions.stem: The potential difference $(V_A - V_B)$ between the points A and B in the given figure is
questions.solution:
Step 1: Walk from A to B along the current $I = 2\ \mathrm{A}$. Across a resistor in the direction of current the potential drops by $IR$.
Step 2: Drop across $2\ \Omega$: $2 \times 2 = 4\ \mathrm{V}$. The cell is crossed from its + plate to its - plate: drop of $3\ \mathrm{V}$. Drop across $1\ \Omega$: $2 \times 1 = 2\ \mathrm{V}$.
Step 3: $V_A - 4 - 3 - 2 = V_B \Rightarrow V_A - V_B = 9\ \mathrm{V}$.
Final Answer: (C) 9 V
Quick Tip: Going from + to − terminal of a cell is a fall of potential equal to its emf, whatever the current direction.

questions.stem: Which one of the following person is in an inertial frame of reference?
questions.solution:
Step 1: An inertial frame is one that is at rest or moves with constant velocity (zero acceleration).
Step 2: A decelerating train, a revolving merry-go-round (centripetal acceleration) and a plane taking off are all accelerated frames; only the bus moving with constant velocity is unaccelerated.
Final Answer: (C) A person (driver) in a bus which is moving with constant velocity.
Quick Tip: Any change in speed or direction makes the frame non-inertial.

options.text: A person (man) in a train which is slowing down to stop.
A person (child) revolving in a merry-go-round.
A person (driver) in a bus which is moving with constant velocity.
A person (pilot) in an aeroplane which is taking off.

questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.stem: Two discs A and B of same material and thickness have radii $R$ and $3R$ respectively. Their moments of inertia about their axis will be in the ratio
questions.solution:
Step 1: Moment of inertia of a disc about its axis: $I = \frac{1}{2}MR^{2}$, with $M = \rho\,(\pi R^{2})\,t$.
Step 2: Same material and thickness, so $M \propto R^{2}$ and hence $I \propto R^{4}$.
Step 3: $\frac{I_A}{I_B} = \left(\frac{R}{3R}\right)^{4} = \frac{1}{81}$.
Final Answer: (C) $1 : 81$
Quick Tip: Do not forget that the mass also changes with radius; $I \propto R^{4}$ for discs of equal thickness.

questions.stem: When an observer moves towards a stationary source with velocity ' $\mathrm{V_1}$ ', the apparent frequency of emitted note is ' $\mathrm{F_1}$ '. When observer moves away from stationary source with velocity ' $\mathrm{V_1}$ ' the apparent frequency is ' $\mathrm{F_2}$ '. If ' v ' is velocity of sound in air and $\frac{\mathrm{F_1}}{\mathrm{F_2}} = 2$, then $\frac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{V_1}}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Step 1: Observer moving, source at rest: towards, $F_1 = f\frac{v + V_1}{v}$; away, $F_2 = f\frac{v - V_1}{v}$.
Step 2: $\frac{F_1}{F_2} = \frac{v + V_1}{v - V_1} = 2 \Rightarrow v + V_1 = 2v - 2V_1$.
Step 3: $v = 3V_1 \Rightarrow \frac{v}{V_1} = 3$.
Final Answer: (C) 3
Quick Tip: For $\frac{v + u}{v - u} = k$, directly $\frac{v}{u} = \frac{k + 1}{k - 1} = \frac{3}{1}$.

questions.stem:
For the following reaction, the particle ' X ' is
$${}_{6}\mathrm{C}^{11} \longrightarrow {}_{5}\mathrm{B}^{11} + \beta + \mathrm{X}$$
questions.solution:
Step 1: Atomic number falls by 1 while mass number stays 11, so a proton changes into a neutron: this is $\beta^{+}$ (positron) decay, $p \to n + e^{+} + \nu$.
Step 2: To conserve energy, momentum and lepton number, $\beta^{+}$ emission is always accompanied by a neutrino, so X is a neutrino.
Final Answer: (B) neutrino
Quick Tip: $\beta^{-}$ decay emits an antineutrino; $\beta^{+}$ decay emits a neutrino.

questions.stem: In fundamental mode, the time required for the sound wave to reach up to closed end of a pipe filled with air is ' $t$ ' second. The frequency of vibration of air column is (Neglect end correction)
questions.solution:
Step 1: For a closed pipe in fundamental mode, $L = \frac{\lambda}{4}$, and the sound travels the length $L$ in time $t$: $L = vt$.
Step 2: $\lambda = 4L = 4vt$.
Step 3: $n = \frac{v}{\lambda} = \frac{v}{4vt} = \frac{1}{4t} = (4t)^{-1}$.
Final Answer: (A) $(4t)^{-1}$
Quick Tip: Time for one wavelength is the period; here $\lambda = 4L$, so period $= 4t$.

questions.stem: A wire has three different sections as shown in figure. The magnitude of the magnetic field produced at the centre ' $O$ ' of the semicircle by three sections together is ( $\mu_0 =$ permeability of free space)
questions.solution:
Step 1: The straight sections (i) and (iii) lie along the line through O (the diameter line), so for every element $d\vec{l} \parallel \vec{r}$ and $d\vec{l} \times \vec{r} = 0$: they give no field at O.
Step 2: A full circular loop gives $\frac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$ at its centre, so the semicircle (ii) gives half of it: $B = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4R}$.
Final Answer: (A) $\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{4\mathrm{R}}$
Quick Tip: A straight wire contributes zero field at any point on its own line (or its extension).

questions.stem: A student measures time for 20 oscillations of a simple pendulum as $30\ \mathrm{s}, 32\ \mathrm{s}, 35\ \mathrm{s}$ and 35 s . If the minimum division in the measuring clock is 1 s , then correct mean time (in second) is
questions.solution:
Step 1: Mean $= \frac{30 + 32 + 35 + 35}{4} = \frac{132}{4} = 33\ \mathrm{s}$.
Step 2: Absolute errors: $|30 - 33| = 3$, $|32 - 33| = 1$, $|35 - 33| = 2$, $|35 - 33| = 2$.
Step 3: Mean absolute error $= \frac{3 + 1 + 2 + 2}{4} = 2\ \mathrm{s}$ (greater than the least count 1 s, so it is retained). Result: $(33 \pm 2)\ \mathrm{s}$.
Final Answer: (A) $(33 \pm 2)$
Quick Tip: Report the larger of the mean absolute error and the least count as the uncertainty.

questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.stem: Light of wavelength ' $\lambda$ ' falls on a metal having work function $\frac{hc}{\lambda_0}$. Photoelectric effect will take place only if ( $\lambda_0$ is the threshold wavelength)
questions.solution:
Step 1: Emission requires photon energy $\ge$ work function: $\frac{hc}{\lambda} \ge \frac{hc}{\lambda_0}$.
Step 2: This gives $\frac{1}{\lambda} \ge \frac{1}{\lambda_0}$, i.e. $\lambda \le \lambda_0$.
Final Answer: (C) $\lambda \leq \lambda_0$
Quick Tip: Threshold frequency is a minimum, so threshold wavelength is a maximum.

questions.stem: For a particle moving in a circle with constant angular speed, which of the following statements is 'false'?
questions.solution:
Step 1: In uniform circular motion the velocity is tangential and the only acceleration is centripetal, $a = \omega^{2}r$, directed towards the centre.
Step 2: Hence velocity and acceleration are perpendicular; (A), (C), (D) are true. There is no tangential acceleration because $\omega$ is constant, so (B) is false.
Final Answer: (B) The acceleration vector is tangent to the circle.
Quick Tip: Tangential acceleration appears only when the speed changes.

options.text: The velocity vector is tangent to the circle.
The acceleration vector is tangent to the circle.
The velocity and acceleration vectors are perpendicular to each other.
The acceleration vector points to the centre of the circle.

questions.stem: In Young's double slit experiment, the distance between screen and aperture is 1 m . The slit width is 2 mm . Light of $6000\mathring{A}$ is used. If a thin glass plate ( $\mu = 1.5$ ) of thickness 0.04 mm is placed over one of the slits, then there will be a lateral displacement of the fringes by
questions.solution:
Step 1: Fringe shift due to a thin plate: $x = \frac{(\mu - 1)tD}{d}$ (independent of $\lambda$); here $d = 2\ \mathrm{mm}$ is the slit separation.
Step 2: $x = \frac{(1.5 - 1)(0.04 \times 10^{-3})(1)}{2 \times 10^{-3}}$.
Step 3: $x = \frac{0.5 \times 0.04}{2} = 0.01\ \mathrm{m} = 1\ \mathrm{cm}$.
Final Answer: (B) 1 cm
Quick Tip: The wavelength is a distractor; it matters only if the shift is asked in number of fringes.

questions.stem: For an ideal diode, in forward and reverse biased condition the resistance is respectively
questions.solution:
Step 1: An ideal diode acts as a closed switch when forward biased: no voltage drop, so resistance is zero.
Step 2: When reverse biased it acts as an open switch: no current, so resistance is infinite.
Final Answer: (D) zero, infinite.
Quick Tip: Ideal diode = perfect one-way switch.

questions.stem: In Young's double slit experiment, when light of wavelength 600 nm is used, 18 fringes are observed on the screen. If the wavelength of light is changed to 400 nm , the number of fringes observed on the screen is
questions.solution:
Step 1: For a fixed screen region, (number of fringes) $\times$ (fringe width) is constant, and fringe width $\beta \propto \lambda$, so $n\lambda$ = constant.
Step 2: $18 \times 600 = n_2 \times 400$.
Step 3: $n_2 = \frac{10800}{400} = 27$.
Final Answer: (B) 27
Quick Tip: Smaller wavelength gives narrower fringes, so more of them fit: $n \propto \frac{1}{\lambda}$.

questions.stem: If $\vec{A} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$, $\vec{B} = -\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$ and $\vec{C} = 2\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} - 8\hat{k}$, then the angle between the vectors $\vec{P} = \vec{A} + \vec{B} + \vec{C}$ and $\vec{Q} = (\vec{A} \times \vec{B})$ is (in degree)
questions.solution:
Step 1: $\vec{P} = (1 - 1 + 2)\hat{i} + (1 + 1 - 2)\hat{j} + (3 + 4 - 8)\hat{k} = 2\hat{i} + 0\hat{j} - \hat{k}$.
Step 2: $\vec{Q} = \vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \hat{i}(1 \cdot 4 - 3 \cdot 1) - \hat{j}(1 \cdot 4 - 3 \cdot (-1)) + \hat{k}(1 \cdot 1 - 1 \cdot (-1)) = \hat{i} - 7\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}$.
Step 3: $\vec{P} \cdot \vec{Q} = 2(1) + 0(-7) + (-1)(2) = 0$, so the vectors are perpendicular.
Final Answer: (C) $90^\circ$
Quick Tip: A zero dot product means $90^\circ$; no need to find the magnitudes.

questions.stem: A coil of self-inductance $L$ is connected in series with a bulb and an a. c. source. Brightness of the bulb decreases when
questions.solution:
Step 1: Current $I = \frac{V}{\sqrt{R^{2} + X_L^{2}}}$ with $X_L = \omega L$; the bulb dims when $X_L$ (hence impedance) increases.
Step 2: Inserting an iron rod increases the permeability of the core, so $L$ and $X_L$ increase and the current falls. Decreasing frequency or reducing turns lowers $X_L$ (bulb brighter); adding a capacitor partly cancels $X_L$.
Final Answer: (A) an iron rod is inserted in the coil.
Quick Tip: $L \propto \mu_r N^{2}$: an iron core raises $L$ greatly.

options.text: an iron rod is inserted in the coil.
frequency of a.c. source is decreased.
number of turns in the coil is reduced.
a capacitance of reactance $(\mathrm{X_C} - \mathrm{X_L})$ is included in the same circuit.

questions.stem: The period of S. H. M. of a particle is 16 second. The phase difference between the positions at $\mathrm{t} = 2\ \mathrm{s}$ and $\mathrm{t} = 4\ \mathrm{s}$ will be
questions.solution:
Step 1: Phase changes at rate $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = \frac{2\pi}{16} = \frac{\pi}{8}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.
Step 2: $\Delta\phi = \omega\,\Delta t = \frac{\pi}{8} \times (4 - 2) = \frac{\pi}{4}$.
Final Answer: (C) $\frac{\pi}{4}$
Quick Tip: $\Delta\phi = 2\pi \frac{\Delta t}{T} = 2\pi \times \frac{2}{16}$.

questions.stem: A body cools from $60^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $40^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in 6 minutes. After next 6 minutes its temperature will be (Temperature of the surroundings is $10^\circ\mathrm{C}$ )
questions.solution:
Step 1: Newton's law (average form): $\frac{\theta_1 - \theta_2}{t} = k\left(\frac{\theta_1 + \theta_2}{2} - \theta_0\right)$. First interval: $\frac{60 - 40}{6} = k(50 - 10) \Rightarrow k = \frac{1}{12}\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$.
Step 2: Second interval: $\frac{40 - \theta}{6} = \frac{1}{12}\left(\frac{40 + \theta}{2} - 10\right) \Rightarrow 40 - \theta = \frac{40 + \theta}{4} - 5$.
Step 3: $160 - 4\theta = 40 + \theta - 20 \Rightarrow 5\theta = 140 \Rightarrow \theta = 28^\circ\mathrm{C}$. (Exact law: excess falls by the same factor $\frac{30}{50} = 0.6$ in equal times, $10 + 30 \times 0.6 = 28^\circ\mathrm{C}$.)
Final Answer: (B) $28^\circ\mathrm{C}$
Quick Tip: In equal time intervals the excess temperature over the surroundings falls by the same ratio.

questions.stem: A parallel beam of light is incident normally on a plane surface absorbing $50\%$ of the light and reflecting the rest. If the incident beam carries 90 W of power, the force exerted by it on the surface is ( $\mathrm{C} =$ velocity of light in air $= 3 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s}$ )
questions.solution:
Step 1: Absorbed power gives force $\frac{P_a}{c}$; reflected power gives $\frac{2P_r}{c}$ (momentum reversed). Here $P_a = P_r = 45\ \mathrm{W}$.
Step 2: $F = \frac{45}{c} + \frac{2 \times 45}{c} = \frac{135}{3 \times 10^{8}}$.
Step 3: $F = 4.5 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N}$.
Final Answer: (A) $4.5 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N}$
Quick Tip: $F = \frac{P}{c}(1 + r)$ where $r$ is the reflected fraction: $\frac{90}{3 \times 10^{8}} \times 1.5$.

questions.stem: A tyre of a vehicle is filled with air having pressure 270 kPa at $27^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The air pressure in the tyre when the temperature increases to $37^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is
questions.solution:
Step 1: Volume of the tyre is constant, so $\frac{P_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2}{T_2}$ with $T_1 = 300\ \mathrm{K}$, $T_2 = 310\ \mathrm{K}$.
Step 2: $P_2 = 270 \times \frac{310}{300}$.
Step 3: $P_2 = 0.9 \times 310 = 279\ \mathrm{kPa}$.
Final Answer: (D) 279 kPa
Quick Tip: Always convert to kelvin before using gas-law ratios.

questions.stem: A $20\Omega$ resistance, 10 mH inductance coil and $15\mu\mathrm{F}$ capacitor are joined in series. When a suitable frequency alternating current source is joined to this combination, the circuit resonates. If the resistance is made $\frac{1}{3}\mathrm{rd}$, the resonant frequency
questions.solution:
Step 1: Resonant frequency of a series LCR circuit: $f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$.
Step 2: It depends only on $L$ and $C$, not on $R$. Changing $R$ alters only the sharpness (Q-factor) and the peak current.
Final Answer: (A) remains unchanged.
Quick Tip: Resistance changes the height and width of the resonance curve, never its position.

questions.stem: If the period of a oscillation of mass ' m ' suspended from a spring is 2 s , then the period of suspended mass ' 4 m ' with the same spring will be
questions.solution:
Step 1: For a spring-mass system $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$, so $T \propto \sqrt{m}$.
Step 2: $T' = 2 \times \sqrt{\frac{4m}{m}} = 2 \times 2 = 4\ \mathrm{s}$.
Final Answer: (D) 4 s
Quick Tip: Quadrupling the mass doubles the period.

questions.stem: The current flowing through an inductor of selfinductance L is continuously increasing at constant rate. The variation of induced e.m.f. (e) verses $\mathrm{dI/dt}$ is shown graphically by figure

Three point charges $+Q, +2Q$ and $q$ are placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle. The value of charge $q$ in terms of $Q$, so that electrical potential energy of the system is zero, is given by
questions.solution:
Step 1: With side $a$, $U = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 a}\left[(Q)(2Q) + (Q)(q) + (2Q)(q)\right]$.
Step 2: $U = 0 \Rightarrow 2Q^{2} + 3Qq = 0$.
Step 3: $q = -\frac{2Q}{3}$.
Final Answer: (C) $\mathrm{q} = -\frac{2}{3}\mathrm{Q}$
Quick Tip: Equal separations let you cancel $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 a}$ and just sum the charge products.

questions.stem: The surface energy of a liquid drop is ' $V$ '. It is sprayed into 1000 equal droplets. The surface energy of all the droplets is
questions.solution:
Step 1: Volume is conserved: $\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3} = 1000 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3} \Rightarrow r = \frac{R}{10}$.
Step 2: Total area $= 1000 \times 4\pi r^{2} = 1000 \times \frac{4\pi R^{2}}{100} = 10 \times 4\pi R^{2}$.
Step 3: Surface energy $\propto$ area, so it becomes $10V$.
Final Answer: (B) 10 V
Quick Tip: Splitting into $n$ drops multiplies surface energy by $n^{1/3}$: $1000^{1/3} = 10$.

questions.stem: When an n-p-n junction transistor is used as an amplifier in common emitter mode,
questions.solution:
Step 1: In CE amplifier the emitter is common to input and output: input between base and emitter, output between collector and emitter, so (C) is correct.
Step 2: The base-emitter junction is forward biased (A wrong), input impedance is low and output impedance high (B wrong), and output is $180^\circ$ out of phase with input (D wrong).
Final Answer: (C) input signal is applied between the base and emitter and the output is obtained between collector and emitter.
Quick Tip: For amplification: emitter-base forward biased, collector-base reverse biased.

options.text: the base emitter junction is reverse biased.
the input impedance is high and the output impedance is low.
input signal is applied between the base and emitter and the output is obtained between collector and emitter.
the input voltage and the output voltage are in phase.

questions.stem: The average force applied on the walls of a closed container depends as $\mathrm{T^{x}}$ where T is the temperature of an ideal gas. The value of $x$ is
questions.solution:
Step 1: Force on a wall $F = PA$, and for a closed (fixed-volume) container $P = \frac{nRT}{V}$.
Step 2: Hence $F = \frac{nRA}{V}T \propto T^{1}$, so $x = 1$.
Final Answer: (A) 1
Quick Tip: Pressure is proportional to $v_{rms}^{2}$, which is proportional to $T$.

questions.stem: A hollow cylinder has a charge of ' $q$ ' $C$ within it. If $\phi$ is the electric flux associated with the curved surface B, the flux linked with the plane surface A will be
questions.solution:
Step 1: By Gauss's law the total flux through the closed cylinder is $\phi_A + \phi_B + \phi_C = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$.
Step 2: By symmetry the two plane faces get equal flux: $\phi_A = \phi_C$, and $\phi_B = \phi$.
Step 3: $2\phi_A = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} - \phi \Rightarrow \phi_A = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} - \phi\right)$.
Final Answer: (D) $\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} - \phi\right)$
Quick Tip: Subtract the known flux from $\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$ and share the rest equally between identical faces.

questions.stem: A diatomic gas $\left(\gamma = \frac{7}{5}\right)$ is compressed adiabatically to volume $\frac{\mathrm{V_0}}{32}$, where $\mathrm{V_0}$ is its initial volume. The initial temperature of the gas is $\mathrm{T_i}$ in kelvin and the final temperature is $\mathrm{xT_i}$ in kelvin. The value of $x$ is
questions.solution:
Step 1: Adiabatic relation: $TV^{\gamma - 1} = $ constant, with $\gamma - 1 = \frac{2}{5}$.
Step 2: $xT_i\left(\frac{V_0}{32}\right)^{2/5} = T_iV_0^{2/5} \Rightarrow x = 32^{2/5}$.
Step 3: $32^{2/5} = (2^{5})^{2/5} = 2^{2} = 4$.
Final Answer: (B) 4
Quick Tip: Choose numbers so the power is easy: $32 = 2^{5}$ pairs with exponent $\frac{2}{5}$.

questions.stem: The coefficient of mutual induction is 2 H and induced e.m.f. across secondary is 2 kV . Current in the primary is reduced from 6 A to 3 A . The time required for the change of current is
questions.solution:
Step 1: $|e| = M\frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} \Rightarrow \Delta t = \frac{M\,\Delta I}{|e|}$.
Step 2: $\Delta t = \frac{2 \times (6 - 3)}{2000} = \frac{6}{2000}$.
Step 3: $\Delta t = 3 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s}$.
Final Answer: (D) $3 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s}$
Quick Tip: Convert kV to V (2 kV = 2000 V) before dividing.

questions.stem: A liquid drop having surface energy $E$ is spread into 729 droplets of same size. The final surface energy of the droplets is
questions.solution:
Step 1: Volume conservation: $R^{3} = 729\,r^{3} \Rightarrow r = \frac{R}{9}$.
Step 2: Total area $= 729 \times 4\pi\frac{R^{2}}{81} = 9 \times 4\pi R^{2}$.
Step 3: Surface energy $\propto$ area, so final energy $= 9E$.
Final Answer: (B) 9 E
Quick Tip: Final energy $= n^{1/3}E$; $729^{1/3} = 9$.

questions.stem: A body is projected vertically from earth's surface with $\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{\mathrm{rd}}$ of escape velocity. The maximum height reached by the body is ( $R =$ radius of earth)
questions.solution:
Step 1: $v = \frac{v_e}{3}$ with $v_e^{2} = \frac{2GM}{R}$, so $\frac{1}{2}v^{2} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{2GM}{9R} = \frac{GM}{9R}$ (per unit mass).
Step 2: Energy conservation: $\frac{GM}{9R} - \frac{GM}{R} = -\frac{GM}{R + h} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{R + h} = \frac{8}{9R}$.
Step 3: $R + h = \frac{9R}{8} \Rightarrow h = \frac{R}{8}$.
Final Answer: (B) $\frac{\mathrm{R}}{8}$
Quick Tip: For $v = kv_e$, $h = \frac{Rk^{2}}{1 - k^{2}} = \frac{R/9}{8/9} = \frac{R}{8}$.

questions.stem: Two planar concentric rings of metal wire having radii $\mathrm{r_1}$ and $\mathrm{r_2}$ $(\mathrm{r_1} > \mathrm{r_2})$ are placed in air. The current I is flowing through the coil of larger radius. The mutual inductance between the coils is given by ( $\mu_0 =$ permeability of free space)
questions.solution:
Step 1: Field at the centre of the larger ring: $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2r_1}$, nearly uniform over the small ring since $r_2 < r_1$.
Step 2: Flux through the smaller ring: $\phi = B\pi r_2^{2} = \frac{\mu_0 I \pi r_2^{2}}{2r_1}$.
Step 3: $M = \frac{\phi}{I} = \frac{\mu_0 \pi r_2^{2}}{2r_1}$.
Final Answer: (B) $\frac{\mu_0 \pi r_2^{2}}{2r_1}$
Quick Tip: Field comes from the big ring (its radius in the denominator); area is of the small ring.

questions.stem: The work done by a gas as it is taken in a cyclic process (shown in graph) is
questions.solution:
Step 1: Work in a cycle = area enclosed. The cycle is the triangle A$(V, P)$, B$(3V, P)$, C$(3V, 4P)$.
Step 2: Area $= \frac{1}{2} \times (3V - V) \times (4P - P) = \frac{1}{2} \times 2V \times 3P = 3PV$.
Step 3: Path A $\to$ B $\to$ C $\to$ A runs anticlockwise on the P-V graph (right, up, then back down-left), so net work by the gas is negative: $W = -3PV$.
Final Answer: (D) -3 pv
Quick Tip: Clockwise cycle on P-V: positive work; anticlockwise: negative.

questions.stem: A conducting sphere of radius ' R ' is given a charge ' $Q$ ' uniformly. The electric field and the electric potential at the centre of the sphere are respectively [ $\varepsilon_0 =$ permittivity of free space]
questions.solution:
Step 1: Charge on a conductor resides on its surface; by Gauss's law the field anywhere inside is zero, so $E_{centre} = 0$.
Step 2: With zero field inside, the potential is constant and equal to the surface value: $V = \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R}$.
Final Answer: (A) zero and $\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R}$
Quick Tip: Zero field does not mean zero potential; it means constant potential.

questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.stem: An inclined plane makes an angle $30^\circ$ with the horizontal. A solid sphere rolling down an inclined plane from rest without slipping has linear acceleration ( $\mathrm{g} =$ acceleration due to gravity) ( $\sin 30^\circ = 0.5$ )
questions.solution:
Step 1: Rolling without slipping: $a = \frac{g\sin\theta}{1 + \frac{K^{2}}{R^{2}}}$; for a solid sphere $\frac{K^{2}}{R^{2}} = \frac{2}{5}$.
Step 2: $a = \frac{g \times 0.5}{1 + \frac{2}{5}} = \frac{0.5g}{7/5}$.
Step 3: $a = \frac{5}{7} \times \frac{g}{2} = \frac{5g}{14}$.
Final Answer: (B) $\frac{5\mathrm{g}}{14}$
Quick Tip: $\frac{5g}{7}$ is $\frac{a}{\sin\theta}$ for a solid sphere; remember to multiply by $\sin 30^\circ$.

questions.stem: Two pipes of lengths $\mathrm{L_1}$ and $\mathrm{L_2}$, open at both ends are joined in series. If ' $f_1$ ' and ' $f_2$ ' are the fundamental frequencies of two pipes, then the fundamental frequency of series combination will be (neglect end correction)
questions.solution:
Step 1: Open pipe fundamental: $f = \frac{v}{2L}$, so $L_1 = \frac{v}{2f_1}$ and $L_2 = \frac{v}{2f_2}$.
Step 2: Joined pipe has length $L_1 + L_2$: $f = \frac{v}{2(L_1 + L_2)} = \frac{v}{\frac{v}{f_1} + \frac{v}{f_2}}$.
Step 3: $f = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{f_1} + \frac{1}{f_2}} = \frac{f_1 f_2}{f_1 + f_2}$.
Final Answer: (C) $\frac{f_1 f_2}{f_1 + f_2}$
Quick Tip: Lengths add, so reciprocals of frequencies add: $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{f_1} + \frac{1}{f_2}$.

questions.stem: A long wire carrying a steady current is bent into a circle of single turn. The magnetic field at the centre of the coil is ' B '. If it is bent into a circular loop of radius ' $\mathrm{r_1}$ ' having ' n ' turns, the magnetic field at the centre of the coil for same current is
questions.solution:
Step 1: Same wire length: $2\pi R = n(2\pi r_1) \Rightarrow r_1 = \frac{R}{n}$. Single turn: $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$.
Step 2: $n$ turns of radius $r_1$: $B' = \frac{n\mu_0 I}{2r_1} = \frac{n\mu_0 I}{2(R/n)} = n^{2}\frac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$.
Step 3: $B' = n^{2}B$.
Final Answer: (C) $n^{2}B$
Quick Tip: One factor $n$ from the turns, another from the smaller radius.

questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.stem: Two spheres each of mass $M$ and radius $R$ are connected with a massless rod of length 4 R . The moment of inertia of the system about an axis passing through the centre of one of the spheres and perpendicular to the rod will be
questions.solution:
Step 1: In the figure the 4R is the distance between the centres of the spheres. Sphere through whose centre the axis passes: $I_1 = \frac{2}{5}MR^{2}$.
Step 2: Other sphere, by the parallel axis theorem: $I_2 = \frac{2}{5}MR^{2} + M(4R)^{2} = \frac{2}{5}MR^{2} + 16MR^{2}$.
Step 3: $I = \frac{2}{5}MR^{2} + \frac{2}{5}MR^{2} + 16MR^{2} = \frac{4 + 80}{5}MR^{2} = \frac{84}{5}MR^{2}$.
Final Answer: (B) $\frac{84}{5}\mathrm{MR^{2}}$
Quick Tip: Use the centre-to-centre distance in the parallel axis term, not the rod length between surfaces.

questions.stem: In Young's double slit experiment, for the $n$th dark fringe ( $\mathrm{n} = 1, 2, 3 \ldots$ ) the phase difference of the interfering waves in radian will be
questions.solution:
Step 1: Dark fringes need path difference $(2n - 1)\frac{\lambda}{2}$ for $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$
Step 2: Phase difference $= \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} \times (2n - 1)\frac{\lambda}{2} = (2n - 1)\pi$.
Final Answer: (C) $(2n - 1)\pi$
Quick Tip: With $n$ starting at 1, use $(2n - 1)$; $(2n + 1)$ fits only when $n$ starts at 0.

questions.stem: A water drop of $0.01\ \mathrm{cm^{3}}$ is squeezed between two glass plates and spreads in to area of $10\ \mathrm{cm^{2}}$. If surface tension of water is 70 dyne $/\mathrm{cm}$ then the normal force required to separate glass plates from each other will be
questions.solution:
Step 1: Film thickness $d = \frac{V}{A} = \frac{0.01}{10} = 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{cm}$. Force to separate the plates: $F = \frac{2TA}{d}$.
Step 2: $F = \frac{2 \times 70 \times 10}{10^{-3}} = 1.4 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{dyne}$.
Step 3: $1\ \mathrm{N} = 10^{5}\ \mathrm{dyne}$, so $F = 14\ \mathrm{N}$.
Final Answer: (B) 14 N
Quick Tip: The thin film's curved edge creates pressure deficit $\frac{2T}{d}$ acting over area $A$.

questions.stem: A null point is obtained at 200 cm on potentiometer wire when cell in secondary circuit is shunted by $5\Omega$. When a resistance of $15\Omega$ is used for shunting, null point moves to 300 cm . The internal resistance of the cell is
questions.solution:
Step 1: With shunt $S$, terminal voltage $= \frac{ES}{S + r} = kl$.
Step 2: $\frac{5E}{5 + r} = 200k$ and $\frac{15E}{15 + r} = 300k$. Dividing: $\frac{15(5 + r)}{5(15 + r)} = \frac{300}{200} \Rightarrow \frac{3(5 + r)}{15 + r} = 1.5$.
Step 3: $15 + 3r = 22.5 + 1.5r \Rightarrow 1.5r = 7.5 \Rightarrow r = 5\ \Omega$.
Final Answer: (C) $5\Omega$
Quick Tip: Write $\frac{S}{S + r} \propto l$ for each case and take the ratio to cancel $E$ and $k$.

questions.stem: A resistance of $200\Omega$ and an inductor of $\frac{1}{2\pi}\mathrm{H}$ are connected in series to a.c. voltage of 40 V and 100 Hz frequency. The phase angle between the voltage and current is
questions.solution:
Step 1: $X_L = 2\pi fL = 2\pi \times 100 \times \frac{1}{2\pi} = 100\ \Omega$.
Step 2: $\tan\phi = \frac{X_L}{R} = \frac{100}{200} = 0.5$.
Step 3: $\phi = \tan^{-1}(0.5)$.
Final Answer: (D) $\tan^{-1}(0.5)$
Quick Tip: The $\frac{1}{2\pi}$ in L is chosen so that $X_L$ equals the frequency in hertz.

questions.stem: A wire of length L , diameter ' d ' density of material ' e ' is under tension ' T ', having fundamental frequency of vibration $\mathrm{n_A}$. Another wire of length 2 L , tension 2 T , density 2 e and diameter 3 d has fundamental frequency of vibration $\mathrm{n_B}$. The ratio $\mathrm{n_B} : \mathrm{n_A}$ is
questions.solution:
Step 1: $n = \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}}$ with $\mu = \frac{\pi d^{2}}{4}e$, so $n \propto \frac{1}{Ld}\sqrt{\frac{T}{e}}$.
Step 2: $\frac{n_B}{n_A} = \frac{L \cdot d}{2L \cdot 3d}\sqrt{\frac{2T/2e}{T/e}} = \frac{1}{6} \times 1$.
Step 3: $n_B : n_A = 1 : 6$.
Final Answer: (C) $1 : 6$
Quick Tip: Mass per unit length depends on diameter squared, so $n \propto \frac{1}{d}$.

questions.stem: ' n ' small spherical drops of same size which are charged to ' $V$ ' volt each coalesce to form a single big drop. The potential of the big drop is
questions.solution:
Step 1: Volume conserved: $R = n^{1/3}r$. Charge conserved: $Q = nq$.
Step 2: Small drop: $V = \frac{kq}{r}$. Big drop: $V' = \frac{kQ}{R} = \frac{knq}{n^{1/3}r}$.
Step 3: $V' = n^{2/3}\frac{kq}{r} = n^{2/3}V$.
Final Answer: (D) $\mathrm{n}^{2/3} \cdot \mathrm{V}$
Quick Tip: For $n$ drops merging: charge $\times n$, radius $\times n^{1/3}$, potential $\times n^{2/3}$, energy $\times n^{5/3}$.

questions.stem: In a transistor (common emitter configuration) the ratio of power gain to voltage gain is ( $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are current ratios)
questions.solution:
Step 1: Power gain = current gain $\times$ voltage gain. In CE configuration the current gain is $\beta = \frac{I_C}{I_B}$.
Step 2: $\frac{\text{power gain}}{\text{voltage gain}} = \frac{\beta A_v}{A_v} = \beta$.
Final Answer: (D) $\beta$
Quick Tip: In CB mode the same ratio would be $\alpha$.

questions.stem: A particle oscillates in straight line simple harmonically with period 8 second and amplitude $4\sqrt{2}\ \mathrm{m}$. Particle starts from mean position. The ratio of the distance travelled by it in $1^{\mathrm{st}}$ second of its motion to that in $2^{\mathrm{nd}}$ second is $\left(\sin 45^\circ = 1/\sqrt{2}, \sin\frac{\pi}{2} = 1\right)$
questions.solution:
Step 1: $x = A\sin\omega t$ with $\omega = \frac{2\pi}{8} = \frac{\pi}{4}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$, $A = 4\sqrt{2}\ \mathrm{m}$.
Step 2: At $t = 1\ \mathrm{s}$: $x = A\sin 45^\circ = \frac{A}{\sqrt{2}} = 4\ \mathrm{m}$. At $t = 2\ \mathrm{s}$: $x = A\sin 90^\circ = 4\sqrt{2}\ \mathrm{m}$ (no turning back before $t = 2\ \mathrm{s}$).
Step 3: Distances: first second $4\ \mathrm{m}$; second second $4\sqrt{2} - 4 = 4(\sqrt{2} - 1)\ \mathrm{m}$. Ratio $= 1 : (\sqrt{2} - 1)$.
Final Answer: (D) $1 : (\sqrt{2} - 1)$
Quick Tip: The particle reaches the extreme at $t = \frac{T}{4} = 2\ \mathrm{s}$, so both intervals are one-way motion.

questions.stem: The length of the compound microscope is 15 cm . The magnifying power for relaxed eye is 25 . If the focal length of eye lens is 6 cm then the object distance for objective lens will be
questions.solution:
Step 1: Relaxed eye: final image at infinity, so the image by the objective is at the eyepiece focus: $L = v_o + f_e \Rightarrow v_o = 15 - 6 = 9\ \mathrm{cm}$.
Step 2: $M = \frac{v_o}{u_o} \cdot \frac{D}{f_e} \Rightarrow 25 = \frac{9}{u_o} \times \frac{25}{6}$.
Step 3: $\frac{9}{u_o} = 6 \Rightarrow u_o = 1.5\ \mathrm{cm}$.
Final Answer: (B) 1.5 cm
Quick Tip: For normal adjustment, tube length $= v_o + f_e$ and eyepiece magnification $= \frac{D}{f_e}$.

questions.stem: The magnetic susceptibility of iron is 5499 . The relative permeability of iron will be
questions.solution:
Step 1: Relative permeability and susceptibility are related by $\mu_r = 1 + \chi$.
Step 2: $\mu_r = 1 + 5499 = 5500$ (dimensionless).
Final Answer: (C) 5500
Quick Tip: $\mu_r$ is a pure number; do not bring in $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$.
